catalog_quote: Stress in Nukna is bounded, falling into a bisyllabic stress window at the beginning of the word. Within this window, stress is trochaic (left- headed). (1) hála ['hʌ.la] ‘almost’ ... ámna ['ʌm.na] ‘man’ (2) kaláhu ['ka.lʌ.hu] ‘three’ ... máriya ['mʌ.ɾi.ja] ‘later’ However, Nukna is a variable stress language that is quantity-sensitive. That is, heavy syllables within the stress window may attract stress (in Nukna, a syllable is considered heavy if it is a closed by a consonant). However, a heavy syllable only attracts stress if the first syllable in the stress window contains the vowel [ʌ]. (3) káyam [kʌ.'yam] ‘enemy’ kárang [kʌ.'ɾaŋ] ‘bamboo’ márum [mʌ.'ɾum] ‘owner’ (4) kisum ['ki.sum] ‘coconut shell’ kuhát ['ku.hʌt] ‘frog’ mukam ['mu.kam] ‘cloud’ ... Heavy syllables outside of the stress window do not attract stress, even if both vowels in the stress window are [ʌ]. (5) sumuyung ['su…

sources.quote: 'Stress in Nukna is bounded, falling into a bisyllabic stress window at the beginning of the word. Within this window, stress is trochaic (left-headed). However, the second syllable in the stress window will attract stress if it is a heavy syllable (CVC) and if the first syllable in the stress window contains the vowel [ʌ]. It is difficult to clearly hear the stress on bisyllabic words that end in a heavy syllable. Stress has not been found to be contrastive. See the Nukna Grammar Sketch (Taylor: 2015) for a more detailed description of stress in Nukna.' Examples: táwi [ˈtʌ.wi], kákáuk [kʌ.ˈkʌ
